summary: This note is a Wikipedia-derived profile of Josip Broz Tito, the Yugoslav communist leader. It covers his early life and military service in World War I, his Comintern and Soviet-era activities, and his leadership in World War II and in the Cold War, including the Non-Aligned Movement and relations with Eastern and Western countries. It also covers his burial in Belgrade and his continuing legacy, such as the annual Brotherhood and Unity relay.
one_line: A Wikipedia-based profile of Yugoslav communist leader Josip Broz Tito, covering his wartime leadership, Cold War diplomacy, and legacy.
key_facts: On 1 January 1967, Yugoslavia was the first communist country to open its borders to all foreign visitors and abolish visa requirements.
In 1967 Tito became active in promoting a peaceful resolution of the Arab–Israeli conflict; his plan called for Arabs to recognize the state of Israel in exchange for territories Israel gained.
Tito was interred in a mausoleum called House of Flowers (Kuća Cveća) in Belgrade, part of a memorial complex in the grounds of the Museum of Yugoslav History.
In 1968 Tito offered Czechoslovak leader Alexander Dubček to fly to Prague on three hours notice if Dubček needed help facing down the Soviets.
In April 1969 Tito removed generals Ivan Gošnjak and Rade Hamović after the invasion of Czechoslovakia, due to the unpreparedness of the Yugoslav army to respond to a similar invasion of Yugoslavia.
On 6 April 1941, German forces, with Hungarian and Italian assistance, launched an invasion of Yugoslavia.
On 27 June 1941, the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia appointed Tito Commander in Chief of all national liberation military forces.
Yugoslavia was the only communist country allowed to have an embassy in Alfredo Stroessner's Paraguay.
On 7 April 1963, the country changed its official name to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.
On 25 March 1915, while in Bukovina, Tito was seriously wounded and captured by the Russians.
Every year a 'Brotherhood and Unity' relay race ends at the House of Flowers in Belgrade on May 25, the final resting place of Tito.
In autumn 1960 Tito met President Dwight D. Eisenhower at the United Nations General Assembly; Tito said neutralism meant 'not taking sides'.
In October 1936, Tito married Austrian comrade Lucia Bauer, but the records of this marriage were later erased.
In 1937 Stalin had the Secretary-General of the CPY, Milan Gorkić, murdered in Moscow, and Tito was subsequently appointed Secretary-General of the still-outlawed CPY.
Tito was instrumental in kick-starting the Non-Aligned Movement, which would function as a 'third way' for countries staying outside the East-West divide.
